avoid:Coming in winter for the food.name: Coming in winter for the food
avoid:Coming in winter for the food.teaser: From November most kitchens are shuttered; the island you read about runs from spring to October
avoid:Coming in winter for the food.story: Walk the Rum quarter on a late-autumn evening and the lanes that held fifty tables in August are dark: chairs stacked behind glass, vine canopies bare, the meltem rattling a shutter. The island empties after the season and very few businesses stay open through the winter; a TGRT report on the New Year rush found the handful that do, and others reopening only because guests asked. The squid is still in the strait and the wine is still in the cellars, but the long meze evening needs a full room and a full kitchen, and from November you cannot count on either.
avoid:Coming in winter for the food.why: Plan the eating trip for late May, June or September, and treat a winter visit as a walk with a bottle, not a table crawl.
facts: Late October: shutters coming down in the Rum quarter, beach businesses packed away, the ferry already on its reduced winter timetable

Come late May to June or in September. In winter, no kept table is confirmed open: call Asmalı Meyhane, Sandal, Nevreste or Ada'm before you cross, and buy from the cellar shops (Talay, Çamlıbağ) to drink on board

avoid:The car ferry on a summer Friday.name: The car ferry on a summer Friday
avoid:The car ferry on a summer Friday.teaser: One GESTAŞ line carries every car to the island, and on a holiday weekend everyone tries it at once
avoid:The car ferry on a summer Friday.story: Everything that reaches Bozcaada by road goes through the pier at Geyikli (Yükyeri) and the GESTAŞ car ferry, a crossing of about 35 minutes. Tickets are sold on the mainland side; there is no ticket office on the island. On long holiday weekends the island fills: in May 2026 the regional press reported it 'doldu taştı', full to overflowing, and bayram bookings close to 100 per cent. The ferry runs hourly in high summer, but from 5 October 2026 the winter timetable cut it to four or five sailings a day, three to four hours apart, so a missed boat now costs an afternoon.
avoid:The car ferry on a summer Friday.why: Leave the car on the mainland and cross on foot on a weekday; the town, the cellars and the near beaches are all within reach without one.
facts: Winter timetable from 5 Oct 2026 (seen Oct 2026, valid to 30 Nov): from Geyikli 08:00, 11:00, 15:00, 19:00, plus 23:00 Friday to Sunday; from Bozcaada 07:00, 10:00, 14:00, 18:00, plus 22:00 Friday to Sunday
Cross as a foot passenger on a weekday, check the day's sailings with the operator first, and in summer ask about the passenger-only sea bus from Çanakkale city (old guide; not re-checked)

avoid:The harbour-front set menu.name: The harbour-front set menu
avoid:The harbour-front set menu.teaser: The tables built for the tour coaches feed volume; the island's real kitchen is a few lanes back
avoid:The harbour-front set menu.story: Bozcaada's money no longer comes from the bottle but from the day-tripper: the old guide counted well over a million visitors a year and summer rooms near full. Some of the harbour-front tables are set up for exactly that crowd, a fixed run of plates timed to the next ferry, laid out for the group rather than cooked for the person. The fish and the squid on the island come from the same strait whichever door you choose; what changes is whether a cook is watching the grill. Your money goes further at the cellar door, at the Wednesday market and at the meyhanes that cook to order.
avoid:The harbour-front set menu.why: Walk two or three lanes up from the water before you sit down; the meze tables that cook to order are there.
facts: The harbour edge by the castle: laminated menus, plates for groups, tables turned for the next boat
Book Asmalı Meyhane, Sandal or Ada'm in the Rum quarter, or Nevreste near the harbour, and order from the meze tray; in the off-season, call ahead

follow:Bozcaada municipality.name: Bozcaada municipality
follow:Bozcaada municipality.teaser: The town hall's own site: where the harvest-festival programme and island notices are posted
follow:Bozcaada municipality.story: Bozcaada Belediyesi is the island's municipality and the body that has run the September grape-harvest festival since the 1990s. Its website is where official notices go first: job calls, public announcements and the programmes of the events it organises. It is written for islanders, in Turkish, and is plain rather than polished, but when you need to know whether the harvest days or a public event are on, the town hall is the source the travel sites copy from.
follow:Bozcaada municipality.why: Check it before planning around a festival date; third-party listings disagree.
facts: The official site of Bozcaada Belediyesi, the island municipality
Announcements (duyurular) and the event programme, especially before the September harvest days

follow:The ferry operator.name: GESTAŞ, the ferry operator
follow:The ferry operator.teaser: The only car ferry to the island: its timetable changes with the season, sometimes twice in a month
follow:The ferry operator.story: GESTAŞ runs the Geyikli to Bozcaada line along with the other Çanakkale island and strait crossings. Its timetable is the one fact every shore plan hangs on, and it moves: hourly in summer, every two hours from mid-September 2026, then four or five sailings a day from 5 October. Weather cancellations and extra holiday sailings are announced at short notice. The company's own site carries the current timetables and online tickets, and it runs a 24-hour call centre.
follow:The ferry operator.why: Check the day's sailings here on the morning you cross, not the week before.
facts: GESTAŞ Deniz Ulaşım, operator of the Geyikli–Bozcaada car ferry; timetables, notices and online tickets
Sefer tarifeleri (timetables) and the cancellation notices; call centre 444 0 752 (seen Oct 2026)

follow:The island's wine.name: GoTürkiye vineyard routes
follow:The island's wine.teaser: The tourism ministry's wine pages put Bozcaada on the Troy wine route, grape by grape
follow:The island's wine.story: GoTürkiye is the Ministry of Culture and Tourism's own travel site, and its vineyard section is the clearest English-language map of where Bozcaada sits in Turkish wine. The island is on its Troy wine route with the mainland vineyards of the Troad, and a separate page walks through the native grapes, including the thin-skinned Vasilaki and the red Karalahna. It is promotional and light on vintages, but it is official, it is in English, and it names the grapes the way the cellar doors will.
follow:The island's wine.why: Read the grape page before the cellar visits, so the names on the labels are already familiar.
facts: The Turkish tourism ministry's vineyard and wine-route pages, with a Bozcaada heritage feature
The Troy wine route, the indigenous grape varieties page, and the Cultural Journeys page on Bozcaada viticulture

listening:No hi-fi listening bar.name: No hi-fi listening bar
listening:No hi-fi listening bar.teaser: No record bar on the island or in Çanakkale that we could find; here the music is live, and seasonal
listening:No hi-fi listening bar.story: We looked for a vinyl or hi-fi listening room on Bozcaada and across the strait in Çanakkale, and found none. An island of about three thousand winter residents does not keep one going. What it has instead is sound you have to be there for: a jazz festival that takes over a monastery yard and a beach for three days in early September, music in the lanes during the harvest days, and in high summer the late bars of the Rum quarter. Out of season the soundtrack is the meltem in the vines and the ferry horn.
listening:No hi-fi listening bar.why: Time the trip for the early-September jazz weekend if music is the point.
facts: Late October: no listening bar open on the island or in Çanakkale that any source lists
See 'Live music on the island' for the Bozcaada Caz Festivali in early September; in summer, the late bar at Bakkal in the Rum quarter

listening:Live music on the island.name: Live music on the island
listening:Live music on the island.teaser: Three stages in early September: a monastery yard, a beach and a free one in town
listening:Live music on the island.story: The Bozcaada Caz Festivali reached its tenth edition in 2026, on the first weekend of September, under the theme 'Geçicilik', impermanence. It spreads over three stages: the yard of the Ayazma monastery above the south coast, the sand at Habbele, and a free stage at the Salhane in town. The bill runs from jazz to electronic, psychedelic and reggae, with players from the UK, the Netherlands, Germany and France beside Turkish names such as Korhan Futacı and Gevende, plus talks, workshops and walks across the island. Outside that weekend, music is a summer thing; at New Year the few meyhanes and bars that open put on their own nights.
listening:Live music on the island.why: The free Salhane stage lets you hear the festival without a ticket.
facts: Ayazma monastery, Habbele beach and the Salhane stage in town
Early September: 4 to 6 September in 2026 (one source says 3 to 5); next edition not yet announced (Oct 2026)
Salhane stage free; ticket prices for the other stages not found

craft:Do this one.name: The harvest at Bağ Bozumu
craft:Do this one.teaser: Nothing on the island clears the bar fully; the closest is picking grapes in the rows at harvest
craft:Do this one.story: We searched for a hands-on class proper to Bozcaada with a named maker you can sign up with: ceramics, weaving, jam, cooking, boatbuilding. None turned up. The nearest thing is the harvest itself. For about four days in September the municipality takes visitors out to the vineyards to cut bunches by hand, the Çavuş and Karalahna knuckled low against the wind, and the grapes come back to town on tractors and carts with music. It is real work in a real crop, open to anyone who turns up, but it is an event, not an apprenticeship: no named master teaches you, and it happens once a year.
craft:Do this one.why: It is the one week you hold the island's grapes in your hand rather than in a glass.
facts: Pick grapes by hand in a working vineyard and follow the harvest back into town
A morning in the vines, during the harvest days in September; 2027 dates not yet announced (Oct 2026)
Not found; no fee is reported for joining the picking
No booking found: watch the municipality's programme, or ask Talay or Çamlıbağ whether you can join their own harvest

craft:Other one.name: Bozcaada Kadın Kooperatifi
craft:Other one.teaser: The island women's cooperative makes the jams and meze the National Geographic coverage singled out
craft:Other one.story: When National Geographic put Bozcaada on its 2026 food list, the Turkish press coverage picked out the jams and meze made by the Bozcaada Kadın Kooperatifi, the island women's cooperative, as part of the island's small-scale local production. This is the craft in its home: preserving the summer's fruit and vegetables in syrup and oil, in the Rum and Turkish kitchen tradition the island shares. You can buy what they make. Missing: we found no open workshop or class where a visitor can learn it with them.
craft:Other one.why: Buy from the cooperative rather than the souvenir shelf, and ask in person whether a session is possible.
facts: Buy jams and meze made by the cooperative; no hands-on session found
No booking channel found; ask at the Wednesday market

craft:Other two.name: Bozcaada's hand-woven cottons
craft:Other two.teaser: The island's old clothing cloth was hand-woven cotton with its own motifs; a university study keeps the record
craft:Other two.story: A 2019 study from Çanakkale Onsekiz Mart University catalogued the heirloom textiles kept in Bozcaada homes: clothing cloth hand-woven in cotton, with motifs the researchers recorded as the island's own. It is the craft that comes closest to being Bozcaada's alone, the work of looms in the island's houses rather than a mainland workshop. Missing: we found no weaver still working on the island and no class to join; what survives is in chests and in the paper.
craft:Other two.why: Read it as a lead: ask in the Rum quarter who still keeps the old cloths.
facts: Nothing hands-on: the record is a published study

craft:What is sold as island-made.name: What is sold as island-made
craft:What is sold as island-made.teaser: 'Island wine' in a plain bottle is not always what it claims: police seized 1,300 litres of fake on Bozcaada
craft:What is sold as island-made.story: The island's reputation sells, and not everything that trades on it is what the label says. In one operation the gendarmerie raided a vineyard house on Bozcaada and seized 1,300 litres of counterfeit wine, with one person detained. Home-batch wine is part of island life, made in small lots for the family, but a plain unlabelled bottle sold over a counter carries no guarantee of grape, maker or safety. The old guide's advice holds for food too: the year-round tourist stalls are not the same thing as the Wednesday producers' market, and the Çavuş grapes and jams are best bought from the people who grow and cook them.
craft:What is sold as island-made.why: Buy wine with a producer's name on it, from the producer.
facts: Unlabelled or hand-labelled 'Bozcaada şarabı' and jams on souvenir shelves around the harbour
Wine from the cellar shops (Talay, Çamlıbağ) or the cellar doors (Corvus, Amadeus); grapes, cheese and tomato jam from the Wednesday market; preserves from the women's cooperative

drink:Çavuş.name: Çavuş
drink:Çavuş.teaser: The island's sweetest eating grape, pressed into a dry white
drink:Çavuş.story: Çavuş is the grape Bozcaada eats: islanders call it the most flavourful of the island's table grapes, big, thin-skinned and fragile. The wineries also press it, alone or with Vasilaki, for dry whites and pale rosés. A grape bred for the fruit bowl is not an obvious candidate for a serious wine, which is exactly why the bottles are worth a glass: expect something light and soft rather than sharp, made to drink young with the meze. Corvus and Talay both make one.
drink:Çavuş.why: Ask for a Çavuş white with the first cold meze, before the reds come out.
facts: A light, soft dry white, sometimes a pale rosé; drink it young and cold
Çavuş, alone or blended with Vasilaki; Bozcaada on the label
"Bir şişe Bozcaada Çavuş": a Corvus or Talay bottling

drink:Vasilaki.name: Vasilaki
drink:Vasilaki.teaser: A thin-skinned white that ripens early on the island and is drunk young
drink:Vasilaki.story: Vasilaki keeps a Greek name from the island's Rum winemakers. It is a white with thin-skinned berries that ripens early on Bozcaada and goes into both dry and sweet wines; the ministry's grape guide is plain that it is not one for the cellar. Writers describe the dry version as acidic and fuller than you expect, one comparing it to a Chardonnay, nearly. The old guide said it grows nowhere else; the sources we found call it Bozcaada's own but do not go that far. Drink it the year after the harvest, with grilled fish.
drink:Vasilaki.why: If a cellar has a sweet Vasilaki, taste it beside the dry one: the same grape, two directions.
facts: Fresh, acidic, fuller than its colour suggests; dry or sweet
Vasilaki, alone or blended with Çavuş; drink the youngest vintage
A dry Vasilaki with the fish, a sweet one with the pastanesi's biscuits

sources.label: Turkey Travel Planner: Turkish wine grapes

drink:Karalahna and Kuntra.name: Karalahna and Kuntra
drink:Karalahna and Kuntra.teaser: Two island reds: one dark and firm, one light and cherry-red, often in the same bottle
drink:Karalahna and Kuntra.story: Karalahna is late-ripening and grown almost only on Bozcaada: deep-coloured, high in acid, firm in tannin. Even its name is argued over, black pumpkin or black cabbage. Kuntra is the same grape the mainland calls Karasakız (also Mavro Kuntra, Sakız Kara); light, with red cherry and redcurrant, it went mostly into the still for brandy until island producers revived it for reds, rosés and sparkling wines. Each covers the other's gap, which is why the cellars so often blend them, or set Karalahna beside Merlot. Corvus's Corpus is the famous one; ask the cellar door for the plain versions too.
drink:Karalahna and Kuntra.why: Taste a straight Kuntra and a Karalahna blend side by side to understand the island's red.
facts: Karalahna: dark, tannic, high acid. Kuntra: pale, light, red cherry and redcurrant
Kuntra may appear as Karasakız; blends read Karalahna–Kuntra or Karalahna–Merlot
A Kuntra rosé with the meze, a Karalahna blend with grilled meat

drink:Rakı.name: Rakı
drink:Rakı.teaser: Not made on the island, but the drink the meze evening is built around
drink:Rakı.story: Bozcaada makes wine; rakı comes from the mainland. Yet under the vine canopies of the meyhanes it is the fixed partner to the cold meze, the raw fish and the grilled squid as they come out in waves. It is an anise spirit, clear in the bottle, that turns cloudy white the moment water goes in. The ritual is slow: a narrow glass, a finger or two of rakı, cold water to cloud it, then ice, and a long evening of small plates between sips. The old guide put it best: the wine is what you take home, the rakı is the meal.
drink:Rakı.why: Order it the island way, with the meze tray, and let the evening run at its pace.
facts: Clear anise spirit that turns milky white with water
A tek (single) or duble (double), with a jug of cold water and a bowl of ice
Rakı first, water to cloud it, ice after; sip between mezes, never as a shot

bars:Bakkal.name: Bakkal
bars:Bakkal.teaser: A cocktail bar on a cobbled side lane: quiet by day, a small dancefloor by two in the morning
bars:Bakkal.story: Bakkal means grocer, and the name is the joke: this is one of the few places on the island that turn into a bar after dark. By day it is fresh juice and quiet tables on a cobbled side lane of the Rum quarter; on a summer night it fills with a young crowd, music up, the lane full. The cocktails lean on what grows here: Hürriyet Daily News sent readers for the ones made with corn poppy and with grapes. It is seasonal, so in late October expect it shut until spring.
bars:Bakkal.why: Go for one cocktail made from island fruit before the music takes over.
facts: Rum quarter, on a side lane near the museum (Lale Sokak in the old record; not confirmed)
Seasonal, roughly April to October, 11:00 to 03:00 (seen May 2026); expect it closed in winter
A corn-poppy or grape cocktail; the old record names the Magnolia
Early evening for a quiet glass; after midnight it is loud

bars:The wine route.name: The wine route
bars:The wine route.teaser: Two cellar shops in town, the bigger cellar doors out in the vines, all inside one island day
bars:The wine route.story: Close to half of Bozcaada is under vine, dry-farmed and trained low as bushes against the meltem, and the island is small enough that the wine route is the island itself. Start in town, where Talay and Çamlıbağ, two old family houses, pour at their shops among the lanes. Then go out into the vines: Corvus by the rows north-west of town, with limited visiting days, and Amadeus to the south, where the winemaker pours himself. In September the air at the cellars smells of must; in late October the rows are bare, and outside summer the tastings are not guaranteed.
bars:The wine route.why: Do the town shops on foot and hire a car or taxi for the cellar doors out in the vines.
facts: The town centre, at the Talay and Çamlıbağ shops
A day, with lunch in town between the shops and the cellar doors
A native-grape tasting: Çavuş, Vasilaki, Karalahna and Kuntra side by side
Water, a hat, and a car or taxi for Corvus and Amadeus; call ahead in October to April, as winter opening is not confirmed

sources.label: GoTürkiye Cultural Journeys: Bozcaada's 3000-year-old viticulture heritage

bars:Çamlıbağ.name: Çamlıbağ
bars:Çamlıbağ.teaser: One of the island's oldest wineries, with roots at the start of the Republic and a shop in town
bars:Çamlıbağ.story: Çamlıbağ is one of Bozcaada's oldest wine houses, its history going back to the first years of the Turkish Republic, when the island's Greek winemakers were starting to leave and take their skills with them. Wine writers note that it and Talay are related families. The old guide gives 1925 and calls it the island's first Muslim-owned winery; we could not find a source for either the date or the claim, so take them as island tradition. The visit is a working shop in town, shelves of native-grape bottles and staff who know them, not a show cellar.
bars:Çamlıbağ.why: Buy here for the boat: the island's grapes from one of its oldest houses, at shop prices.
facts: Town-centre sales shop (Çamlıbağ Şarapları Satış Mağazası)
Hours not found; tastings are a summer thing, so call ahead from October to April
Native-grape wines: Çavuş, Vasilaki, Karalahna, Kuntra
Not needed for the shop; ask ahead for a tasting
